subject: Creativity
title: Psychological Safety: Google's Secret to Team Creativity
description: A short lesson to help you apply Psychological Safety: Google's Secret to Team Creativity.

hook.text: Google studied 180 teams to find what makes some creative and others not. It wasn't talent, experience, or resources.

buildup.text: Project Aristotle found the best predictor of team innovation was psychological safety: people could take risks.

discovery.text: In psychologically safe teams, people propose wild ideas, admit mistakes, and challenge each other.

climax.text: Leaders create safety through behavior: admitting their own mistakes, asking genuine questions, responding to bad news.

punchline.text: The best teams aren't fearless. They feel safe enough to speak.

details.summary: Google's Project Aristotle studied 180 teams and found that psychological safety, the belief that you will not be punished for mistakes or speaking up, was the single most important factor in team effectiveness. Teams where members felt safe to take risks consistently outperformed those that did...
details.whyItMatters: Psychological safety transforms team dynamics from political maneuvering to honest collaboration. It is the foundation that enables creative risk-taking, constructive disagreement, and learning from failure.
takeaways: Psychological safety was the top predictor of team effectiveness at Google
It enables creative risk-taking and honest disagreement
Leaders create psychological safety through modeling vulnerability

faq.question: How do you measure psychological safety?
faq.answer: Amy Edmondson's research measures it through team member agreement with statements like I feel safe to take a risk on this team and If I make a mistake on this team it is held against me. The aggregate response reveals the team's psychological safety level.

faq.question: Can psychological safety be created deliberately?
faq.answer: Yes. Leaders create it by responding constructively to mistakes, asking for input genuinely, acknowledging their own errors publicly, and ensuring that speaking up is rewarded rather than punished. It requires consistent behavior over time to build trust.
